name: Adam Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do the underground side, mostly. Cables under the old part of the city, some of them laid before I was born, wrapped in paper and oil. A normal day, I get a fault location from control, we dig or lift the cover, and I go down in the pit and make the joint. It's slow, careful work, and I'm good at it, everyone knows that. What wears me out is the traffic, the cones, the drivers shouting at us, and my back after six hours bent in a hole.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Has technology changed much of what you do?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not much down there. They've got a fancy fault-finding van now that's quicker than the old way, I'll give them that. But I don't use these AI things, never have. My son put one on my phone and I took it off again. I don't need a computer to tell me how to joint a cable I've jointed a thousand times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, nobody knows anything. I'm not one for big opinions on this stuff. At work I'd probably just shrug and get on with the next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things carry on, which is fine by me. I'll be honest, I'm not rich, we've got very little in the bank. But that's how it's been for years and it's nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep doing the job, keep the overtime when it comes. Maybe look at some extra weekend standby to chip at the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you bought the house late. How does that play out now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We bought at 45, when the kids were already teenagers, because we'd been renting for years. So the mortgage runs till I'm 75, which is a joke, I know. Every month it's the mortgage, the bills and then whatever's left, and usually there isn't much left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what's the plan for the mortgage after 65?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll do part-time or consulting, maybe help a contractor with jointing jobs, for a few years after I stop full-time. Samira might keep her pharmacy hours. That's the plan, anyway, I don't think too hard about it.

S0.say: I'd say nobody really knows anything about this. At work I'd shrug and get on with the next job.
S0.think: Privately, things carry on and that's fine. We've got very little in the bank, but that's been true for years and has nothing to do with computers.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and takes overtime when it comes. Considers extra weekend standby shifts to chip away at the mortgage.
S0.feel: Calm, as if nothing much has changed.
S0.quote: So the mortgage runs till I'm 75, which is a joke, I know.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is matter-of-fact and avoids big opinions. The striking fact is a mortgage running to 75, which means his plan depends on working part-time well past retirement. He doesn't seem to look closely at that plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some jobs will change and some won't, and mine's one that won't, not much. People like to make a fuss. I wouldn't post anything, I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm safe enough. I'm senior, I'm the best jointer in the district, and nobody's building a robot to crawl into a pit under a busy road in the next few years. I'd worry more for the office people than for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. If they bring in some new kit, I'll learn what I have to, but I'm not volunteering. I'd keep the weekend standby for the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Maybe a small itch in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the old cables keep you safe. Why's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every pit is different. You open it and there's a gas main where the drawings say there isn't, or a cable from 1962 that nobody mapped. You need a person who's seen it before. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company asked you to learn new equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it, I wouldn't make trouble. But I'd want someone to show me properly, not just hand me a manual. I'm slow with screens and I don't mind admitting it.

S1.say: I'd say some jobs will change and some won't, and mine won't change much. I wouldn't post anything, as I never do.
S1.think: Privately I think I'm safe enough as the best jointer in the district. No one's building a robot to crawl into pits under busy roads soon, and office jobs are more at risk.
S1.do: Carries on as normal, learning new kit only if required and never volunteering. Keeps weekend standby shifts for the extra money.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small itch at the back of his mind.
S1.quote: You open it and there's a gas main where the drawings say there isn't, or a cable from 1962 that nobody mapped.
S1.fieldNote: His confidence rests on the messiness of old underground networks, which is a real point. He would go along with change but wouldn't seek it. He's open about being slow with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now three pictures about full AGI, at different speeds. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and I'd want to know who let it happen so fast. I'm not political, but I'd want someone in government to explain what happens to people like me. At work, I think everyone would go quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be stuck. If a robot can do my job in two years, I'm 60 with a mortgage till 75 and about a month of money. There's maybe one other underground contractor in this city, and they'd be in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything but the basics, straight away. I'd ask Samira about more hours at the pharmacy. And I'd talk to the bank early about the mortgage, before we fall behind, which I've never done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly frightened. I'm not used to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up just thinking about it. If I lose the job, we can't pay, and at 60 nobody gives you a new loan. We might have to sell and rent again, after all that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you even look for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really don't know. Driving, maybe, but the robots would be driving too, wouldn't they? I've only ever done this.

S2.say: I'd say it's mad and I'd want to know who let it happen so fast. I'd want someone in government to explain what happens to people like me.
S2.think: Privately I'd be stuck at 60 with a mortgage till 75 and about a month of money. The one other underground contractor in the city would be in the same boat.
S2.do: Cuts spending to basics straight away and asks his wife about more pharmacy hours. Talks to the bank about the mortgage early, before falling behind.
S2.feel: Properly frightened, which he says he's not used to.
S2.quote: Driving, maybe, but the robots would be driving too, wouldn't they? I've only ever done this.
S2.fieldNote: This is where his calm breaks. The late mortgage turns a job loss into the risk of losing the house. He has no fallback and admits it plainly, which seemed hard for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, all right, five years, that's time to sort something out. I'd want the government and the company to come up with a plan for older workers. I'd say that at work if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still bad for me, but not as bad. Five years gets me to 63, so I'd have less of the mortgage left and could maybe find something part-time. It's tight, very tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start cutting back now and put whatever I could into savings, a little every month. I'd stop helping Karim with his car payments. I'd ask the union about any early retirement deals, though I'm not a big union man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years make you think about learning something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Something practical, like the electrical inspection side, if it wasn't too much screen work. I'd want to see others try it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to stop asking me for car money, for a start. And to look at work that's still going to be there, though I don't know what that is.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to sort something out, and I'd want the government and company to plan for older workers. I'd say that at work if asked.
S3.think: Privately it's still bad but less so, since I'd reach 63 with less mortgage left. Maybe I could find part-time work, but it's very tight.
S3.do: Starts cutting back and saving a little each month, and stops helping his son with car payments. Asks the union about early retirement deals.
S3.quote: I'd tell him to stop asking me for car money, for a start.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time softens the blow but doesn't change his basic position: no fallback, mortgage to 75. He's willing to consider electrical inspection, but only after watching others. His pragmatism shows in leaning on the union despite not being a union man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to get ready. I'd probably not say much more. It'd feel far away to most people at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not as safe as it sounds for me. I'd be retired from the company, but I was counting on part-time jointing work until 75 to pay off the house. If robots do that by 2036, the plan's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, but I'd try to pay extra on the mortgage now, even small amounts, so less is left when I'm 68. I'd keep my head down and wait to see what happens with the robots. And I'd talk to Samira about downsizing at some point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but slow. Like a leak you know is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 68 then. Are you still worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because of the house. My retirement plan isn't really a retirement, it's more work. And that's exactly the work that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would you do differently, with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay down the mortgage, and maybe move to a smaller place before the robots arrive rather than after. It'd kill Samira to leave the garden, though. We'd see.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to get ready. It would feel far away to most people at work.
S4.think: Privately it's not as safe as it sounds, because I was counting on part-time jointing until 75 to pay off the house. If robots do that by 2036, the plan's gone.
S4.do: Keeps working and pays a little extra on the mortgage now. Waits to see how robots develop and talks with his wife about downsizing at some point.
S4.feel: A slow, steady anxiety, like a leak he knows is there.
S4.quote: My retirement plan isn't really a retirement, it's more work. And that's exactly the work that goes.
S4.fieldNote: This was the surprise: unlike most people his age, the ten-year picture still worries him because his plan depends on work after 65. He only realised this while talking. Downsizing is on the table but painful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be 60 with a mortgage till 75 and about a month in the bank, and we'd probably lose the house. What would help is something for the mortgage, like the bank or the government pausing payments for people who lose their jobs to this, and an early pension for people over 60.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how long a robot lasts in a wet pit full of mud. I've seen good tools rust in a month down there. I'll believe it when I see one come back up still working.

headlineQuote: I'll believe it when I see one come back up still working.
portrait: Adam Haddad is a 58-year-old underground cable jointer in an old city, quietly proud of being the best in his district and uninterested in AI tools. He and his wife Samira bought their house at 45, so the mortgage runs till he's 75, and they have about a month of savings. He stays calm through a plateau and steady change, sure that messy old pits will always need someone like him. Fast AGI frightens him because it could cost them the house. Even the ten-year picture leaves him anxious, because he realised his retirement plan depends on part-time jointing work until 75.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because at 60 with a mortgage till 75 and about a month of savings, they'd probably lose the house.
whatWouldHelp: Mortgage payment pauses from the bank or government for people who lose their jobs to this, and an early pension for people over 60.
